section_summary: This final section consists chiefly of cross-reference notes and reports concerning Japanese petroleum purchases, industrial concessions, fishing, surveying, and intelligence-gathering in Mexico during 1939. It includes a badly degraded despatch about competing Japanese oil interests and a naval attaché report on possible Japanese involvement in Baja California salt concessions. The section closes with a reference to Japanese surveying and mineral-acquisition activities in Michoacán and Guerrero.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the Mexico visit of Tomonori Nakano and Shigeo Tajika
subfiles.about: The note refers to a report on Nakano and Tajika's visit to Mexico and their return to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch gives a comprehensive account of the two Japanese visitors and identifies Tajika with Okura & Co. in Ginza, Tokyo. Its enclosures included an October 11 Valley Sunday Star clipping and a photographic copy of a Japanese-language letter found on Nakano that mentioned the Standard Oil Company and Wilmington.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Abraham Z. Phillips's flight to Poza Rica with a Japanese party
subfiles.about: The note refers to Despatch No. 9378 concerning a flight over the Poza Rica petroleum region by Phillips and Japanese visitors led by Tomonori Nakano.
subfiles.summary: A considerable number of photographs were reportedly taken during the flight. The referenced despatch also summarized information Phillips supplied to the Commercial Attaché about two separate Japanese groups pursuing petroleum interests in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 9378 on competing Japanese petroleum interests in Mexico
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, U.S. Embassy in Mexico
subfiles.about: The despatch records information from Abraham Z. Phillips about rival Japanese groups seeking Mexican petroleum supplies and related infrastructure.
subfiles.summary: Despite extremely degraded OCR, the despatch describes competing Japanese interests negotiating for Mexican crude oil, with financing or purchasing arrangements apparently linked to the Japanese Navy. It discusses proposed pipelines, terminals, transportation privileges, and a refinery whose construction in Japan might take a year or more. Phillips believed one Japanese group was attempting to displace another from existing contracts and offered to provide further information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the proposed use of Mexican fuel oil
subfiles.about: Instruction No. 2746 requested clarification regarding the destination and intended use of fuel oil being sold to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: The Department referred to Mexico's telegram No. 341 of October 24 and asked whether the reported fuel oil belonged to a previously known shipment. It also requested information on whether a Japanese naval vessel might still collect a cargo of Mexican oil.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on a 50,000-ton Mexican oil sale to Japan
subfiles.about: The note reports the commercial chain and financing behind a sale of 50,000 metric tons of Mexican oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pemex reportedly sold the oil to La Laguna, S.A., which resold it to the Pacific Petroleum Company of Japan. The Japanese Navy was said to provide the money, and the transaction was reportedly payable in cash.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese fishing activities in Mexican waters
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of the Interior, Jackson
subfiles.about: The note identifies a report on Japanese fishing activities prepared by a Bureau of Fisheries agent in California.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report concerned Japanese fishing operations in Mexican waters. It was prepared by C. B. Tendrick, the Bureau of Fisheries agent stationed at San Pedro, California.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese fishing off Baja California
subfiles.from: Fishermen's Co-operative Association of San Pedro, John Rusich
subfiles.about: The note refers to fishermen's information concerning Japanese fishing operations off the Baja California coast.
subfiles.summary: Members of the Fishermen's Co-operative Association gathered information about Japanese activities off Baja California. The referenced letter summarized their observations and was associated with John Rusich of San Pedro.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese oil activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of the American Republics, Bursley
subfiles.about: The memorandum transmitted excerpts and a report about individuals involved in Japanese petroleum activity in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: It attached excerpts from an October 23 letter and an August 1 report prepared by Roscoe B. Gaither for the War Department. The material mentioned geologist Joe Weckstein, William Smith, and two Japanese identified as Mr. Suri and Dr. Turuhagua.

subfiles.title: Naval Attaché's Report No. 247-39 on Japanese interest in Baja California salt deposits
subfiles.from: W. M. Dillon, U.S. Naval Attaché, Mexico
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, U.S. Navy Department
subfiles.about: The report relays an overheard Mexico City conversation suggesting Japanese interest in concessions to exploit Baja California salt deposits.
subfiles.summary: A Commercial Attaché's office clerk overheard Nagabuchi and other Japanese and Mexican participants discuss salt concessions at San Felipe, including concessions held by Isais, a reported payment of 200,000 pesos, shipping capacity, dredging, and Colonel Cantú's interest. One concession was said to have been obtained from President Cárdenas, and the participants preferred an 8,000-ton vessel over a 10,000-ton vessel because it would require less dredging. The attaché believed Nagabuchi belonged to the San Francisco branch of Mitsui & Company.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese activities in Michoacán and Guerrero
subfiles.about: The note refers to a military attaché report on Japanese surveying, mineral acquisitions, and financial activities in Michoacán and Guerrero.
subfiles.summary: Amonaki and Ichiguito were reportedly posing as ranchers while possessing high-grade engineering, surveying, and photographic equipment and drawing drafts on the Laguna Oil Company in Mexico City. Japanese personnel were observed surveying properties at Las Truchas, while Mexican intermediaries tried to interest Kenneth S. Littlejohn in iron deposits. Japanese interests also reportedly secured options for feldspar and 10,000 tons of scrap iron for shipment to Japan.
